title: unsafe, honestly
intro: `unsafe` does not turn the compiler off. It unlocks a short list of operations the compiler cannot check, such as reading through a raw pointer, and moves the proof to you: you write the conditions down and promise they hold. You can write whole programs without it. It is there for talking to C, for building the pieces the standard library is made of, and for data structures the borrow checker cannot express. The craft is to keep the promise small and wrap it in a function that is safe to call.

coming_from.go: Go has the `unsafe` package: `unsafe.Pointer` and `unsafe.Add` give you pointer arithmetic, as the program above shows. A file that imports `unsafe` can use it anywhere, with no block marking each use. Rust marks every use and expects a `// SAFETY:` comment saying why it is sound.
coming_from.kotlin: Kotlin has no `unsafe` keyword. On the JVM the low-level tools are Java's: `sun.misc.Unsafe` and the `java.lang.foreign` API that the program above uses. They are library calls, not a language boundary: no keyword or block marks the code that uses them, though the JDK now prints warnings.
coming_from.python: Python has no raw pointers in the language. The `ctypes` module is the escape hatch, and its documentation says that indexing a `ctypes` pointer can "access or change arbitrary memory locations". Rust draws that line in the language: the `unsafe` keyword, checked by the compiler.
coming_from.typescript: TypeScript has no pointers and no way to read memory by address. Its escape hatches (`as`, `any`) switch off the type checker but not memory safety. The nearest thing to the program above is a `DataView` over an `ArrayBuffer`, which is bounds-checked.
coming_from.java: Java hides raw memory behind APIs, not a keyword: `sun.misc.Unsafe` (now warning that it will be removed) and the `java.lang.foreign` API that the program above uses, which is bounds-checked. The JDK now warns when you use either, but they are library calls. In Rust the keyword marks each block, and calling an `unsafe fn` is itself unsafe.
coming_from.csharp: C# has an `unsafe` keyword for pointers, and the compiler refuses it unless the project sets `AllowUnsafeBlocks`. By default `unsafe` there places no obligation on callers; in Rust an `unsafe fn` does. The program above avoids the keyword with the `Unsafe` class.
coming_from.c: C has no safe subset marked in the language: pointer arithmetic, indexing past the end and use after free all compile. Rust's `unsafe` adds a boundary, not a new power: inside it you can do what C does (with stricter rules for references), outside it the compiler checks.
coming_from.cpp: C++ has the same unchecked pointers as C, plus checked alternatives such as `at()` that you have to choose. Rust inverts the default: the checked forms are what you get, and the unchecked ones are behind `unsafe`, with a name (`get_unchecked`) that says so.

notes: `unsafe` does not turn off the borrow checker. A reference inside an `unsafe` block is still checked. The keyword unlocks five main operations (the Reference lists a few more): dereference a raw pointer, call an `unsafe fn`, use a `static mut`, implement an `unsafe trait`, and read a `union` field.
Making a raw pointer is safe. Reading or writing through it is not, because only you know whether it is null, dangling, misaligned or aliased.
An `unsafe fn` lists conditions its caller must meet. An `unsafe` block says "I checked them, here is why". Write the why in a `// SAFETY:` comment, and the conditions in a `# Safety` section.
The point is a safe abstraction: a function whose checks make every call sound, so callers never write `unsafe`. The standard library's `Vec` and `split_at_mut` work this way.

gotcha.title: Reading through a raw pointer without `unsafe`
gotcha.looks_fine: You made a pointer to the first element and want the second, as you would in C, with Go's `unsafe` package or with Python's `ctypes`: move the pointer along and read.
gotcha.rust_sees: `p.add(1)` is a call to an `unsafe` function (it needs the result to stay inside the same allocation) and `*` on a raw pointer is a dereference. Both are among the operations that only an `unsafe` block allows, so the compiler reports each.
gotcha.why: The compiler cannot see what `p` points at. It could be null, freed, misaligned or already borrowed, and a read through it would then be undefined behavior. An `unsafe` block says you checked, and the `// SAFETY:` comment is where you write what you checked.

go.says: Go compiles this and prints `second: 20`. The `import "unsafe"` line is the marker; the compiler asks for no block and no reason at the place of use.

kotlin.says: Kotlin on the JVM has no pointers to dereference. The JVM's raw-memory APIs are Java's, and they are calls, not syntax.

python.says: Python prints `second: 20`. `ctypes` pointers can be indexed with no marker, and its documentation says that you can use them to "access or change arbitrary memory locations".
python.code:
import ctypes

prices = (ctypes.c_int * 3)(10, 20, 30)
p = ctypes.cast(prices, ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_int))
second = p[1]
print(f"second: {second}")

typescript.says: TypeScript has no pointers. The nearest thing is a `DataView`, which reads by byte offset inside an `ArrayBuffer`.

java.says: Java has no pointers in the language. Reading memory by address goes through `sun.misc.Unsafe` or `java.lang.foreign`, which are library calls and not syntax.

csharp.says: C# refuses this too: `CS0214`, pointers may only be used in an unsafe context. It has the same idea, and it adds a project switch (`AllowUnsafeBlocks`) before an `unsafe` block compiles at all.

kotlin.code:
import java.lang.foreign.MemorySegment
import java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout

fun get(a: IntArray, i: Int) = a.getOrNull(i)?.let { "Some($it)" } ?: "None"

fun main() {
    val prices = intArrayOf(10, 20, 30)
    // a MemorySegment is a bounds-checked view of memory, read by byte offset
    val second = MemorySegment.ofArray(prices).get(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, 4)
    println("second, read by offset: $second")
    println("get(1): ${get(prices, 1)}")
    println("get(9): ${get(prices, 9)}")
}
